---
title: "What the field expects: AI competency frameworks"
---

A **competency** is something a doctor should be able to know or do by a given
stage of training. A **competency framework** is a list of them, usually
grouped into areas called domains. Medical schools use frameworks to decide
what to teach, and accrediting bodies use them to decide what to require.

For AI, there is no single agreed framework yet. Several groups have proposed
one, and they agree more than they differ. This appendix lists the ones worth
knowing, says where each stands, and shows how this course is built on them.

Use it in three ways:

- When you [plan your four weeks](../chapters/plan-your-learning.qmd), these
  are the sources your research with ChatGPT should find. Compare its list
  with this one.
- When a residency program or a school asks what you know about AI, these are
  the areas they are likely to mean.
- When the AAMC publishes its competencies (below), compare them with your
  plan and with the [coverage table](../index.qmd#competency-coverage) in the
  preface.

Last checked: October 12, 2026. This area changes fast. Check the links for
newer versions.

## The AAMC

The Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) represents US and Canadian
medical schools. It has three pieces of work on AI.

**AI Competencies Across the Learning Continuum.** A national set of AI
competencies for medical school, residency, and practice, supported in part by
the Josiah Macy Jr. Foundation. It is **not yet published.** The AAMC
circulated a first draft for comment in April 2026 and a second in June 2026.
Its stated aim is that learners "develop a shared foundation in core AI
concepts; understand the ethical, legal, and professional implications of
AI-enabled care; and are prepared to effectively use, evaluate, and
collaborate around AI technologies". The same page reports that the share of
US and Canadian MD and DO schools teaching AI rose from 53% in 2023 to 77% in
2024. [AAMC project
page](https://www.aamc.org/about-us/medical-education/ai-competencies).

**Principles for the Responsible Use of AI in and for Medical Education.**
Version 2.0, July 2025. Seven principles for how *schools* use AI, such as
keeping a human-centered focus, providing equal access, and protecting data
privacy. They are rules for institutions, not a list of what you should be
able to do. [AAMC
principles](https://www.aamc.org/about-us/mission-areas/medical-education/principles-ai-use).

**AI Competencies for Medical Educators.** A framework for *faculty*, written
by an AAMC regional group (the Central Group on Educational Affairs) in 2025.
It has eight domains, from understanding AI to continuous professional
development. That last domain asks faculty to find their own knowledge gaps
and make a learning plan, which is what the [planning
chapter](../chapters/plan-your-learning.qmd) asks of you.
[Framework (PDF)](https://www.aamc.org/media/86881/download?attachment).

The AAMC's international committee on AI (IACAI), run through its MedBiquitous
program, has also published integration frameworks for medical education,
including a matrix of recommendations focused on medical students.
[IACAI page](https://www.medbiq.org/initiatives/international-advisory-committee-artificial-intelligence).

## Other US bodies

**Accreditation (LCME).** The Liaison Committee on Medical Education accredits
US MD programs. In October 2025 it presented a proposed revision of its
curriculum standard. The proposed element on patient care would require
"education and experiential learning ... in the appropriate use of artificial
intelligence and other emerging technologies in diagnosis and patient
management". The LCME lists this as a topic not in the 2025 to 2026
standards. It is a proposal, not yet a requirement. Note the word
*experiential*: the proposal asks for practice, not only lectures.
[LCME
presentation (PDF)](https://lcme.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/LCME_LSL_2025_10-8-25_FINAL.pdf).

**The AMA.** In November 2025 the American Medical Association adopted policy
to develop model AI learning objectives and teaching materials for medical
schools. As of this writing it has not published the objectives. Its free
seven-part *AI in Health Care* series on the AMA Ed Hub is written for
students. [AMA
announcement](https://www.ama-assn.org/press-center/ama-press-releases/ama-adopts-policy-advance-ai-literacy-medical-education);
[AMA ChangeMedEd AI
series](https://www.ama-assn.org/education/changemeded-initiative/ai-medical-education).

**The Macy Foundation conference.** A 2025 conference with the AAMC and the
ACGME, which accredits residencies, made five recommendations. The first is to
put AI curricula and competencies in place [@pmid:40424523].

## Published frameworks

These were developed by researchers and published in peer-reviewed journals.
Each was built by asking experts, by reviewing earlier proposals, or both.

| Framework | How it was made | What it contains | Why it is useful to you |
|---|---|---|---|
| Russell et al., *Academic Medicine*, 2023 [@pmid:36731054] | Interviews with 15 experts | 6 domains, 25 subcompetencies, for all health professionals | The most-cited US framework. Its domains are short and readable; start here |
| Hunt et al., *npj Digital Medicine*, 2026 [@pmid:42120544] | Review of 54 studies from 22 countries | 7 domains, 37 competencies, 170 learning objectives | The widest summary of what has been proposed for medical students. Most of its sources were opinion pieces, not studies |
| Lee et al., *Academic Medicine*, 2024 [@pmid:38207056] | Two expert rounds plus a national survey of students and faculty in South Korea | 6 domains, 36 competencies | Separates *essential* from *optional*: most experts rated data science and AI research optional for graduates |
| Singla et al., *npj Digital Medicine*, 2024 [@pmid:39557985] | Three survey rounds with 18 Canadian experts | 82 of 107 competencies rated essential | Includes communication and collaboration, not only knowledge |
| DECODE, Car et al., *JAMA Network Open*, 2025 [@pmid:39888625] | Two survey rounds with experts from many countries | 4 domains, 19 competencies; 33 required and 145 optional learning outcomes | Covers digital health generally, with AI inside it. Shows how to split a small required core from a large optional set |

: Five published frameworks. Numbers are from each paper's abstract. {#tbl-frameworks}

Russell's six domains give a sense of how these frameworks are written. A
health professional should be able to:

1. explain what AI is and describe its uses in health care;
2. explain how social, economic, and political systems shape AI tools, and how
   that affects justice, equity, and ethics;
3. carry out clinical encounters that use AI to build patient-centered care
   plans;
4. evaluate AI tools for quality, accuracy, safety, fit to the setting, and
   bias;
5. analyze and adapt to changes in teams, roles, and workflows when AI tools
   arrive;
6. keep learning about AI tools through continuing education and practice
   improvement.

## What they agree on

Across these frameworks, the same areas come up again and again:

- **Foundations:** what AI and machine learning are, how a chatbot produces an
  answer, and why it can be confidently wrong.
- **Checking:** judging an AI answer, and the evidence for an AI tool, before
  relying on it.
- **Fairness:** where bias comes from, and who a tool may fail.
- **Ethics, law, and professionalism:** privacy, consent, who is responsible,
  how tools are regulated, and keeping your own skills.
- **Using it in practice:** AI in real clinical work, with the doctor still
  deciding.
- **Talking with patients:** explaining when and how AI is part of their care.

Data science and building AI tools appear too. Two of the frameworks above
(Lee and DECODE) treat them as optional for a medical graduate, and this
course does the same.

## How this course uses them

The course's own list of ten competencies, numbered AIM-1 to AIM-9 plus AIM-X,
was built from the frameworks above. Each chapter's objectives box names the
ones it serves, and the [coverage table](../index.qmd#competency-coverage) in the
preface shows which chapters teach which. The numbers stay fixed so the course
can be compared with the AAMC set when it is published.

| ID | Area | Closest match in the frameworks above |
|---|---|---|
| AIM-1 | Foundations of AI and data | Russell 1; Hunt, theory and foundations; Lee 2 |
| AIM-2 | Checking AI tools and their answers | Russell 4; Hunt, critical appraisal |
| AIM-3 | Bias, equity, and social effects | Russell 2; Hunt, ethics |
| AIM-4 | Ethics, law, regulation, and professionalism | Hunt, ethics, law, and professionalism; Lee 3 |
| AIM-5 | Using AI in clinical work | Russell 3; Hunt, clinical applications; Lee 4 |
| AIM-6 | Talking with patients about AI | Singla, communication; Russell 3 in part |
| AIM-7 | Workflow and implementation (optional) | Russell 5 |
| AIM-8 | Health data science (optional) | Lee 5; DECODE, health data science |
| AIM-9 | Research and scholarship (optional) | Hunt, research and innovation; Lee 6 |
| AIM-X | Professional identity and keeping up | Russell 6 |

: The course's competencies and where each comes from. AIM-1 to AIM-6 are the core of the design; AIM-7 to AIM-9 are optional extensions; AIM-X runs through every week. In fall 2026, AIM-3 is taught in a menu chapter, not a core one (see the preface). {#tbl-aim-crosswalk}

Talking with patients about AI is the area this course weights most
differently from the frameworks. Of the five in @tbl-frameworks, only Singla
names communication as an area of its own; the others include it, if at all,
inside wider domains. The course gives it a core week, because it is a conversation you will have in residency
whether or not you use AI yourself.
